title: Recovering After Ransomware
learningObjective: Sequence recovery using containment, clean restoration sources, identity assurance, validation and monitored return to service.
format: 16:9 educational motion-graphics explainer with narration, separate captions and no autoplay audio
visualStyle: Deep navy/charcoal with restrained cyan/electric-blue highlights, limited purple accents, high contrast, stable typography and reduced-motion transitions.

scenes.name: Scenario setup
scenes.visual: A ransomware incident has been contained. Several production servers are encrypted, the backup platform was reachable from part of the affected environment, and an offline backup set is available. Executives want the customer portal restored first. The incident team has not yet validated the backup set or rotated potentially exposed credentials.
scenes.direction: Use a fictional organization, synthetic people and generic systems. Do not expose real identity, secrets or operational infrastructure.

scenes.name: Decision frame
scenes.visual: Sequence recovery using containment, clean restoration sources, identity assurance, validation and monitored return to service.
scenes.direction: Show the decision context and the relevant business/security trade-off. Avoid unsupported claims.

scenes.name: Recommended response
scenes.visual: Option A: Validate and protect clean backup sources, establish a trusted recovery environment, address compromised identities and access paths, restore prioritized services in a controlled order, test integrity and security, then monitor closely before declaring recovery. Correct. Recovery depends on trustworthy restoration sources, a clean environment, identity/access remediation, prioritized validation and monitoring.
scenes.direction: Animate a safe, high-level decision sequence; do not provide attack steps or sensitive operational detail.

scenes.name: Trade-offs
scenes.visual: Option B: The newest backup may also be encrypted, compromised or contaminated. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof. Option C: Payment does not guarantee decryption, recovery or prevention of data disclosure. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof. Option D: Stopped encryption does not prove attacker access or persistence is gone. Review the evidence, use approved organizational controls and avoid treating an alert or familiar message as proof.
scenes.direction: Present the alternatives as decision cards and explain their risks without depicting an actual attack.

scenes.name: Takeaway
scenes.visual: Follow the organization’s recovery plan, validate offline or otherwise trusted backups, rebuild or restore in a clean environment, reset affected credentials and tokens as appropriate, prioritize services by business impact, test security and integrity, and monitor after restoration. Recovery is not simply restoring files; it is returning services to a known-good, validated and monitored state.
scenes.direction: End with concise defensive action and keep text on screen long enough to read.

narration: Scenario: Ransomware encrypted production servers. An offline backup exists, but it has not been validated; credentials may be exposed. Safest response: validate clean backups, establish a trusted recovery environment, remediate identities, restore prioritized services, test and monitor. Option B is unsafe because The newest backup may also be encrypted, compromised or contaminated. Option C is unsafe because Payment does not guarantee decryption, recovery or prevention of data disclosure. Option D is unsafe because Stopped encryption does not prove attacker access or persistence is gone. In practice: follow the recovery plan and confirm integrity and security before return to service. Key takeaway: restore only to a known-good, monitored state.
